title: Spotify Data Tutorial
text:
Spotify Data Tutorial
This package allows users to:

Load Spotify data
Clean and prepare datasets
Analyze artist and song patterns
Generate recommendations


Getting Started
To begin using the dataset, follow this link to download the raw CSV file. This dataset contains nearly 170,000 songs and was obtained through the Spotify API before Spotify enhanced security and limited features in 2024. After downloading the file, load it into your program.


Code
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')


Make sure the CSV file is in your data/ folder or another accessible location.
Install the package by running uv add stat386-spotify-project in the terminal.


Data Cleanup
Once the data is loaded, it is time for some basic cleanup. The artists column is formatted as a list to account for songs with multiple artists or featured collaborators. This makes analysis more difficult, so the first step is to clean that column.


Code
from spotify_tools.clean import fix_artists

df = fix_artists(df)


This function separates the artists from the list into separate entries in the dataframe, making the data much easier to manipulate.
Because 170,000 songs is a large amount of data to work with, this analysis narrows the dataset by removing classical or instrumental artists. In addition, artists with fewer than 40 songs are excluded because they do not provide enough data for meaningful individual analysis.


Code
from spotify_tools.clean import reduce_list

df = reduce_list(df)


Next is some optional data cleaning. The column_cleaning() function converts the duration_ms column to seconds and changes the explicit column from 1 and 0 values to Yes and No. The dataset is then sorted by artist name, and the variables used in this analysis are selected. Additional columns are excluded for consistency and performance.


Code
from spotify_tools.clean import column_cleaning

df = column_cleaning(df)

df = df.sort_values(by ='artists').reset_index(drop = True)
df = df[['name', 'artists', 'year', 'duration_s', 'tempo', 'acousticness', 'energy', 'valence', 'key', 'popularity', 'explicit']]
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['name', 'artists']).reset_index(drop=True)




Basic Analysis
After the data has been cleaned, you can begin the analysis. The primary questions in this project focus on artist consistency and broader trends in music. Because the dataset includes several useful audio features, it provides multiple ways to explore how consistent artists are across their catalogs. A good starting point is to view summary statistics for an individual artist.


Code
from spotify_tools.analysis import artist_summary

artist_summary(df, artist = "Drake")


Running this command with a valid artist name returns summary statistics for that artist.
You can also measure each artist’s variability by using artist_variability(). This function calculates the standard deviation of key audio features for each artist and combines them into an overall variability score.


Code
from spotify_tools.analysis import artist_variability

artist_variability(df)


Additional commands for analysis: - top_songs(df, feature, n) → Returns top N songs ranked by a feature
- feature_trend(df, feature) → Shows how a feature changes over time
- feature_correlations(df) → Displays a correlation matrix of audio features
All of these functions can be imported from the spotify_tools.analysis package.


Extra Features
One feature added during app development was the ability to find songs similar to a selected track. The recommend_similar() command does exactly that. Running the command below returns n songs that are similar to the song you choose.


Code
from spotify_tools.recommend import recommend_similar

recommend_similar(df, song_name = "God's Plan", n = 5)



Important Note
When using functions that require inputs such as feature names, artist names, or song titles, pass those values as strings in quotation marks.

text:
Code
def column_cleaning(df):
    # Convert milliseconds into seconds and rename the column
    df = df[df['duration_ms'] > 53000]
    df['duration_ms'] = df['duration_ms']/1000
    df = df.rename(columns = {'duration_ms' : 'duration_s'})

    df['explicit'] = df['explicit'].map({1: 'Yes', 0: 'No'})
    return df


The Spotify API stores song length in milliseconds by default. This function converts those values to seconds so they are smaller and easier to interpret. It also changes the explicit column from 1 and 0 values to Yes and No.


Code
def reduce_list(df):
    df = df.groupby('artists').filter(lambda x: len(x) >= 40).reset_index(drop = True)
    df = df.groupby('artists').filter(lambda x: x['year'].nunique() >= 10)
    df = df.groupby('artists').filter(lambda x: x['acousticness'].mean() <= .75)
    return df


This function applies three filters to the dataset. The first removes artists with fewer than 40 songs. The second removes artists with fewer than 10 unique years. The final filter removes highly acoustic artists, which often captures classical or instrumental catalogs. Together, these filters make the data more useful for individual artist analysis, especially in the app.


Code
def fix_artists(df):
    # Separate the lists in the artist column
    df['artists'] = df['artists'].apply(ast.literal_eval)
    # One row per artist
    df = df.explode('artists')
    return df


This function makes the DataFrame easier to work with. The artists column is originally stored as a list when a song has multiple artists. For analysis and visualization, it is more useful to separate that list into individual entries.





Code
def artist_summary(df, artist):

    df = df[df['artists'] == artist]

    return df.describe()[['duration_s', 'energy', 'acousticness', 'tempo']]


This function uses the built-in describe() method to create a table of summary statistics for the selected variables.


Code
def feature_trend(df, feature):

    df = df.copy()
    df[feature] = pd.to_numeric(df[feature], errors='coerce')

    return df.groupby('year')[feature].mean().reset_index()


This function accepts a selected feature and returns each year along with that feature’s average value. It is useful for showing how specific aspects of music have changed over time.


Code
def top_songs(df, feature, n=10):

    df = df.copy()

    # Check column exists
    if feature not in df.columns:
        raise ValueError(f"{feature} is not a valid column")

    # Convert to numeric safely
    df[feature] = pd.to_numeric(df[feature], errors='coerce')

    # Drop missing values
    df = df.dropna(subset=[feature])

    # Remove duplicates
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['name', 'artists'])

    # Sort and select top n
    top = df.sort_values(feature, ascending=False).head(n)

    # Return clean output
    return top[['name', 'artists', feature]]


This function takes a selected feature and returns the top songs ranked by that feature.


Code
def song_variability(df):

    features = ['duration_s', 'energy', 'acousticness', 'tempo', 'valence']

    grouped = df.groupby('artists')[features].std()

    grouped['overall_variability'] = grouped.mean(axis=1)

    return grouped.sort_values('overall_variability', ascending=False)


This function measures artist consistency. It uses five variables, calculates each artist’s standard deviation for those variables, and then computes overall variability as the mean of those standard deviations. This helps identify which artists are the most and least variable across those features.


Code
def feature_correlations(df):

    features = ['duration_s', 'energy', 'acousticness', 'tempo', 'valence']

    return df[features].corr()


This function uses duration_s, energy, acousticness, tempo, and valence, then applies the built-in correlation method to create a 5 x 5 matrix showing the relationships among those features.





Code
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity


FEATURE_COLS = [
 'energy', 'acousticness',
    'tempo', 'valence'
]
def recommend_similar(df, song_name, n=5):

    df = df.copy()

    # Convert to numeric
    for col in FEATURE_COLS:
        df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce')

    df = df.dropna(subset=FEATURE_COLS).reset_index(drop=True)

    if song_name not in df['name'].values:
        raise ValueError("Song not found")

    # Feature matrix
    X = df[FEATURE_COLS].values

    # Get the selected song vector
    idx = df[df['name'] == song_name].index[0]
    song_vec = X[idx].reshape(1, -1)

    # 🔥 ONLY compute similarity to this one song
    sim_scores = cosine_similarity(song_vec, X).flatten()

    # Get top matches
    top_idx = sim_scores.argsort()[::-1][1:n+1]

    return df.iloc[top_idx][['name', 'artists']]


This function returns n songs that are most similar to a selected song. It uses the cosine_similarity() function from sklearn to measure similarity in a multidimensional feature space.

#Load in Libraries
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from spotify_tools import recommend_similar

#Plot formatting
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": (0, 0, 0, 0),
    "axes.facecolor": (0, 0, 0, 0),
    "savefig.transparent": True
})

st.set_page_config(page_title="Artist Exploration", layout='wide')

#Load in data
DATA_PATH = 'app_data.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH)


This first section of the app loads the required packages, imports the custom recommend_similar function, formats plot backgrounds to match the app’s style, and reads in the cleaned dataset used for all visuals and tables.


Code
#Creates a unique list for every artist
artist_list = df['artists'].unique().tolist()
artist_list.insert(0, 'All Artists')

#Title and artist selector
st.title("Spotify Artist Exploration")
artist = st.selectbox('Select an artist:', options=artist_list)


This section creates the app title and the interactive dropdown menu. The dropdown includes every unique artist plus an All Artists option so users can choose between a full-dataset view and a specific artist view.


Code
#ALL ARTISTS
if artist == 'All Artists':
    st.dataframe(df)
    tab1, tab2, tab3 = st.tabs(['Length', 'Acousticness', 'Tempo'])

    acous_avg = df.groupby('year')['acousticness'].mean().reset_index()
    durat_avg = df.groupby('year')['duration_s'].mean().reset_index()
    tempo_avg = df.groupby('year')['tempo'].mean().reset_index()


When All Artists is selected, the app displays the complete dataframe and creates three tabs for Length, Acousticness, and Tempo. It also calculates average values by year so the scatterplots can show how each feature changes over time.


Code
    # Song length
    with tab1:
        col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
        # Scatterplot
        with col1:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.scatter(durat_avg['year'], durat_avg['duration_s'] , color='#1DB954')
            ax.set_title('Average Song Length by Year')
            ax.set_xlabel('Year')
            ax.set_ylabel('Length (in seconds)')
            ax.set_ylim(0,400)
            st.pyplot(fig)
        # Histogram
        with col2:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.hist(x = df['duration_s'], color = '#1DB954', bins = 1000)
            ax.set_title('Distribution of Song Length')
            ax.set_xlim(left = 100, right = 700)
            ax.set_xlabel('Length (in seconds)')
            ax.set_ylabel('Count')
            st.pyplot(fig)

    # Acousticness
    with tab2:
        col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
        # Scatterplot
        with col1:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.scatter(acous_avg['year'], acous_avg['acousticness'] , color='#1DB954')
            ax.set_title('Average Acousticness by Year')
            ax.set_xlabel('Year')
            ax.set_ylabel('Acousticness')
            st.pyplot(fig)
        # Histogram
        with col2:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.hist(x = df['acousticness'], color = '#1DB954', bins = 1000)
            ax.set_title('Distribution of Song Acousticness')
            ax.set_xlabel('Acousticness')
            ax.set_ylabel('Count')
            ax.set_ylim(bottom = 0, top = 600)
            st.pyplot(fig)

    # Tempo
    with tab3:
        col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
        with col1:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.scatter(tempo_avg['year'], tempo_avg['tempo'] , color='#1DB954')
            ax.set_title('Average Tempo by Year')
            ax.set_xlabel('Year')
            ax.set_ylabel('Tempo (Beats Per Minute)')
            st.pyplot(fig)
        with col2:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.hist(x = df['tempo'], color = '#1DB954', bins = 800)
            ax.set_title('Distribution of Song Tempo')
            ax.set_xlabel('Tempo (Beats Per Minute)')
            ax.set_xlim(50, 220)
            st.pyplot(fig)


Each of the three tabs in the All Artists view follows the same two-column layout. The left column shows a scatterplot of that feature’s yearly average over time using precomputed averages (durat_avg, acous_avg, and tempo_avg). The right column shows a histogram of that feature across every song in the full dataset, giving the user a sense of its overall distribution.


Code
# INDIVIDUAL ARTISTS
else:
    df_selected = df[df['artists'] == artist].reset_index()
    df_selected = df_selected.groupby('year').filter(lambda x: len(x) >= 3).reset_index(drop=True)

    st.dataframe(df_selected)

    song = st.selectbox("Pick a song:", df_selected['name'])
    if st.button("Recommend"):
        recs = recommend_similar(df, song)
        st.dataframe(recs)


When a single artist is selected, the app filters the dataset to that artist, keeps years with at least three songs, and shows the resulting table. It also lets the user choose a song and click Recommend to return similar songs using the recommendation function from the package.

        with col2:
             fig, ax = plt.subplots()

    with tab2:
        col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
        with col1:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.scatter(df_selected['year'], df_selected['acousticness'] , color='#1DB954')
            ax.set_title(f'Acousticness of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Release Year')
            ax.set_ylabel('Acousticness')
            st.pyplot(fig)

        with col2:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.hist(x = df_selected['acousticness'], color = '#1DB954', bins = 50)
            ax.set_title(f'Distribution of the Acousticness of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Acousticness')
            ax.set_ylabel('Count')
            st.pyplot(fig)
    with tab3:
        col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
        with col1:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.scatter(df_selected['year'], df_selected['tempo'] , color='#1DB954')
            ax.set_title(f'Tempo of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Release Year')
            ax.set_ylabel('Tempo (Beats Per Minute)')
            st.pyplot(fig)

        with col2:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.hist(x = df_selected['tempo'], color = '#1DB954', bins = 50)
            ax.set_title(f'Distribution of the Tempo of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Tempo (Beats Per Minute)')
            st.pyplot(fig)


This final section builds the visual analysis area for an individual artist. In tab1, the app shows a scatterplot of song length by release year and a histogram of that artist’s song-length distribution. In tab2, it repeats that pattern for acousticness, showing both change over time and the feature distribution. In tab3, it does the same for tempo, including units in beats per minute. Each tab uses two side-by-side columns so users can compare trend and distribution at the same time.

             st.pyplot(fig)

    with tab2:
        col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
        with col1:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.scatter(df_selected['year'], df_selected['acousticness'] , color='#1DB954')
            ax.set_title(f'Acousticness of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Release Year')
            ax.set_ylabel('Acousticness')
            st.pyplot(fig)

        with col2:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.hist(x = df_selected['acousticness'], color = '#1DB954', bins = 50)
            ax.set_title(f'Distribution of the Acousticness of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Acousticness')
            ax.set_ylabel('Count')
            st.pyplot(fig)
    with tab3:
        col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
        with col1:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.scatter(df_selected['year'], df_selected['tempo'] , color='#1DB954')
            ax.set_title(f'Tempo of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Release Year')
            ax.set_ylabel('Tempo (Beats Per Minute)')
            st.pyplot(fig)

        with col2:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots()
            ax.hist(x = df_selected['tempo'], color = '#1DB954', bins = 50)
            ax.set_title(f'Distribution of the Tempo of Songs by {artist}')
            ax.set_xlabel('Tempo (Beats Per Minute)')
            st.pyplot(fig)


This final section builds the visual analysis area for an individual artist. In tab1, the app shows a scatterplot of song length by release year and a histogram of that artist’s song-length distribution. In tab2, it repeats that pattern for acousticness, showing both change over time and the feature distribution. In tab3, it does the same for tempo, including units in beats per minute. Each tab uses two side-by-side columns so users can compare trend and distribution at the same time.

title: Top 200 Utah Restaurants
text: As a foodie, I wanted to rank the top 200 restaurants in Utah using a composite score built from Google ratings and review counts. Restaurant rankings are usually subjective, but by combining a quality signal (rating) with a popularity signal (number of reviews), it’s possible to surface places that are both highly reviewed and widely visited. This project documents how I gathered, cleaned, and ranked that data.

title: Top 200 Utah Restaurants
text: As a foodie, I wanted to rank the top 200 restaurants in Utah using a composite score built from Google ratings and review counts. Restaurant rankings are usually subjective, but by combining a quality signal (rating) with a popularity signal (number of reviews), it’s possible to surface places that are both highly reviewed and widely visited. title: Top 200 Utah Restaurants
text:
Motivating Question
According to Google, what are the “best” restaurants in Utah?

title: Top 200 Utah Restaurants
text:
Ethics and Data Collection Practice
I gathered the restaurant data ethically by:

Using the Google Places API — an official, documented access method — with an authenticated API key
Collecting only business-level metadata needed for the analysis (no personal data)
Practicing responsible request behavior: pagination limits, pauses between calls, timeouts, and error handling

title: Top 200 Utah Restaurants
text:
Summary of Steps

Define the goal — identify the top 200 Utah restaurants using a data-driven composite score
Collect data — query the Google Places API across multiple Utah cities using paginated requests with polite delays
Clean — remove duplicate businesses (by place_id), drop records with missing ratings, and filter out entries with zero reviews
Transform — calculate a composite score for each restaurant and rank the full list
Export — keep only the top 200 rows, validate quality, and save to CSV

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Music is a uniquely measurable art form. Through the Spotify API, nearly every song can be quantified by audio features such as tempo, energy, acousticness, and valence. This project explores a dataset of approximately 170,000 Spotify songs to answer the following core questions:

How consistent are artists in their sound across their catalog?
How have key audio features changed over time?
Can we build a tool to recommend similar songs based on audio characteristics?

The result is a Python package (spotify_tools) and an interactive Streamlit web application that allow users to explore these questions visually and interactively.

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Music is a uniquely measurable art form. Through the Spotify API, nearly every song can be quantified by audio features such as tempo, energy, acousticness, and valence. This project explores a dataset of approximately 170,000 Spotify songs to answer the following core questions:

How consistent are artists in their sound across their catalog?
How have key audio features changed over time?
Can we build a tool to recommend similar songs based on audio characteristics?

The result is a Python package (spotify_tools) and an interactive Streamlit web application that allow users to explore these questions visually and interactively.

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Data
The dataset was obtained through the Spotify API prior to Spotify’s security enhancements in 2024. It contains approximately 170,000 songs and includes the following audio features used in this analysis:



Feature
Description




duration_s
Song length in seconds


tempo
Beats per minute


acousticness
Confidence measure of acoustic sound (0–1)


energy
Perceptual intensity and activity (0–1)


valence
Musical positivity (0–1)


popularity
Spotify popularity score (0–100)


explicit
Whether the song contains explicit content

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Data Cleaning
The raw dataset required several cleaning steps before analysis could begin.

Separating Artists
In the raw data, the artists column stores multiple artists as a Python list within each row, to account for collaborations and features. The fix_artists() function expands this list so each artist gets its own row, making grouping and filtering by artist possible.


Code
from spotify_tools.clean import fix_artists

df = fix_artists(df)




Filtering the Artist List
With 170,000 songs, the dataset includes many artists with only a handful of songs or a very narrow date range. Those cases do not work well for meaningful individual artist analysis. The reduce_list() function applies three filters to address this:

Removes artists with fewer than 40 songs
Removes artists active for fewer than 10 unique years
Removes artists with a high average acousticness (≥ 0.75), which filters out classical and instrumental catalogs



Code
from spotify_tools.clean import reduce_list

df = reduce_list(df)




Column Standardization
Song duration is converted from milliseconds to seconds, and the explicit column is converted from binary integers (1/0) to readable labels (Yes/No). The dataset is then sorted, trimmed to the relevant columns, and deduplicated.


Code
from spotify_tools.clean import column_cleaning

df = column_cleaning(df)

df = df.sort_values(by='artists').reset_index(drop=True)
df = df[['name', 'artists', 'year', 'duration_s', 'tempo', 'acousticness',
         'energy', 'valence', 'key', 'popularity', 'explicit']]
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['name', 'artists']).reset_index(drop=True)

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Analysis

Artist Summary Statistics
The first form of analysis is a per-artist summary. The artist_summary() function returns descriptive statistics for an artist’s key audio features, providing a quick snapshot of an artist’s average sound and range.


Code
from spotify_tools.analysis import artist_summary

artist_summary(df, artist="Drake")




Artist Variability
A central question of this project is: how consistent is an artist’s sound? The song_variability() function answers that question by calculating the standard deviation of five key features for each artist and averaging them into a single overall variability score. A high score indicates an artist who changes their sound frequently, while a low score indicates a more uniform catalog.


Code
from spotify_tools.analysis import song_variability

song_variability(df)




Feature Trends Over Time
Music itself changes over time. The feature_trend() function groups the dataset by year and calculates the mean of a selected feature for each year, making it easy to observe how aspects like tempo or acousticness have shifted across decades.


Code
from spotify_tools.analysis import feature_trend

feature_trend(df, feature="energy")




Top Songs by Feature
The top_songs() function accepts any audio feature and returns the top-ranked songs for that feature. This is useful for identifying the loudest, fastest, or most acoustic tracks in the dataset.


Code
from spotify_tools.analysis import top_songs

top_songs(df, feature="tempo", n=10)




Feature Correlations
To understand how audio features relate to one another, the feature_correlations() function generates a correlation matrix across the five primary features. This reveals relationships such as the well-known negative correlation between acousticness and energy.


Code
from spotify_tools.analysis import feature_correlations

feature_correlations(df)

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Song Recommendation
The recommend_similar() function provides a simple but effective recommendation engine. Given a song name, it uses cosine similarity to find the n most similar songs in the dataset based on four audio features: energy, acousticness, tempo, and valence.
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two feature vectors in a multidimensional space. Songs with a small angle between their feature vectors are treated as more similar, regardless of the magnitude of their feature values.


Code
from spotify_tools.recommend import recommend_similar

recommend_similar(df, song_name="God's Plan", n=5)

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Interactive App
The project is accompanied by an interactive Streamlit web application that makes these analyses accessible without writing any code.

App Features
The app opens with a dropdown menu containing every artist in the cleaned dataset, plus an All Artists option.
All Artists view: This view displays the full dataset and provides three tabs: Length, Acousticness, and Tempo. Each tab shows a scatterplot of that feature’s yearly average and a histogram of its overall distribution.
Individual Artist view: This view filters the dataset to the selected artist and displays that artist’s songs in a table. The same three tabs appear, now showing artist-specific trends and distributions. In addition, the user can select one of that artist’s songs and click Recommend to get five similar songs from across the full dataset, powered by the cosine similarity recommendation function.

title: Spotify Music Analysis: Exploring Artist Consistency and Song Similarity
text:
Conclusion
This project demonstrates that audio features from the Spotify API can be used to meaningfully characterize and compare artists, track how music has evolved over time, and identify similar songs. The custom Python package (spotify_tools) turns this analysis into reusable functions, while the Streamlit app makes the results accessible to a broader audience.
Future directions could include:

Adding more audio features to the recommendation engine (e.g., danceability, loudness)
Clustering artists by audio profile
Comparing different time periods or music genres
Using a larger, continuously updated dataset via a re-authorized Spotify API connection

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
Simple linear regression is one of the most fundamental statistical techniques that allows us to predict one variable using another. Whether you’re predicting which country will return humans to the moon first based on recent technological advances, or studying the relationship between movie box office success and production budgets, linear regression is a valuable tool.
In this tutorial, you’ll learn the mathematics behind simple linear regression, how to implement it in Python, and how to interpret your results. By the end, you’ll be able to build your own predictive models with confidence. Let’s dive in!

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
Simple linear regression is one of the most fundamental statistical techniques that allows us to predict one variable using another. Whether you’re predicting which country will return humans to the moon first based on recent technological advances, or studying the relationship between movie box office success and production budgets, linear regression is a valuable tool.
In this tutorial, you’ll learn the mathematics behind simple linear regression, how to implement it in Python, and how to interpret your results. By the end, you’ll be able to build your own predictive models with confidence. Let’s dive in!

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
What is Simple Linear Regression?
Simple linear regression models the relationship between two variables using a straight line. The equation is:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \epsilon\]
Where: - \(y\) is the dependent variable (what we’re predicting) - \(x\) is the independent variable (what we’re using to predict) - \(\beta_0\) is the y-intercept - \(\beta_1\) is the slope - \(\epsilon\) is the error term
The goal is to find the best values for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that minimize the sum of squared errors:
\[SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
where \(\hat{y}_i\) represents our predicted values.

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
Sample Dataset
Let’s work with a simple example: predicting exam scores based on hours studied. Here’s our dataset:



Student
Hours Studied (x)
Exam Score (y)




1
2
65


2
3
70


3
4
75


4
5
82


5
6
85


6
7
90

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
Implementing Linear Regression in Python
Now let’s implement this in Python using scikit-learn. First, we’ll need to import our libraries and prepare our data:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Our data from the table above
hours_studied = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]).reshape(-1, 1)
exam_scores = np.array([65, 70, 75, 82, 85, 90])

# Create and train the model
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(hours_studied, exam_scores)

# Get the coefficients
intercept = model.intercept_
slope = model.coef_[0]

print(f"Intercept (β₀): {intercept:.2f}")
print(f"Slope (β₁): {slope:.2f}")
print(f"Equation: y = {intercept:.2f} + {slope:.2f}x")

# Make a prediction
hours = 5.5
predicted_score = model.predict([[hours]])
print(f"\nPredicted score for {hours} hours: {predicted_score[0]:.2f}")

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
Interpreting the Results
When you run this code, you’ll get output similar to: - Intercept (β₀): ~55.08 - Slope (β₁): ~5.06
This means that for every additional hour studied, the exam score increases by approximately 5.06 points. The intercept suggests a baseline score of about 55.08 when study time is zero (though this may not be practically meaningful).
The prediction tells us that a student who studies 5.5 hours would likely score around 83 points on the exam.

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
Conclusion
Congratulations! You’ve just learned the fundamentals of simple linear regression. You now understand the mathematical foundation behind the technique, how to implement it in Python using scikit-learn, and how to interpret your results.
Simple linear regression is a powerful starting point for statistical modeling. While real-world problems often require more complex approaches, mastering this technique gives you a solid foundation for understanding more advanced statistical methods.

title: Simple Linear Regression in Python: A Beginner’s Guide
text:
Next Steps
Ready to practice? Here’s what you can do:

Try it yourself: Use this code with your own data. Think of two variables that might be related
Visualize your results: Add matplotlib code to plot your regression line
Explore further: Learn about R-squared values to measure model performance

Remember, the best way to learn statistics is by doing. Start small, experiment often, and don’t be afraid to make mistakes.
